title: Score thresholds and abstention
summary: A cutoff decides which retrieved chunks the model may see, and abstention is what the system does when nothing clears the bar. Both depend on scores that are not probabilities.
useIf: Wrong answers cost more than missing answers, or your corpus cannot answer every question users ask.
avoidIf: You would rely on a hard-coded score constant that nobody recalibrates, or you have no labelled unanswerable queries to test it on.

explain.md: Retrieval always returns something. A **cutoff** drops weak chunks, and **abstention** turns an empty or weak shortlist into an honest answer such as 'not found', a clarifying question or a hand-off. The hard part is choosing the signal. Each score has its own scale and its own drift.

head: Signal
Scale
Caution
rows: The distribution shifts with infrastructure and model updates, so use coarse cutoffs only [[r3]]
Drops weak matches before fusion, even when fewer than `k` remain. Specific to the embedding model [[r35]]
Reflects rank agreement and list count, not relevance. Never cut on it [[r1]]

steps.title: Gate
steps.md: Count chunks above the cutoff and compare the gap to the top score.

steps.title: Weak
steps.md: Broaden: rewrite, more candidates or another source.

steps.title: None
steps.md: Abstain: say not found, ask a question or hand off.

explain.md: **Calibration is a measurement, not a guess.** Build a golden set of answerable and unanswerable queries. For each cutoff, record how many answerable queries are still answered (coverage) and how many unanswerable queries are answered anyway (false answers). Pick the point that matches the cost of each error, and recheck after every model or service update. Relative signals such as the gap between the top score and the next, or the number of chunks above the cutoff, move less than absolute scores, though you must still calibrate them (author suggestion). Anthropic's guidance adds the generation side: give the model explicit permission to say it does not know [[r41]]. Corrective RAG goes further by scoring retrieval quality and triggering a different action when it is weak [[r19]].

explain.title: Silent drift
explain.md: A cutoff that worked at launch can quietly turn into 'always abstain' or 'never abstain' after a model update. Track the abstention rate and score percentiles as dashboards and alerts.

whereToUse: Medical, legal and financial assistants where a wrong answer is worse than no answer
Support bots that must hand off to a person when the knowledge base has no answer
Citation-required systems that refuse to answer without evidence
Pipelines that escalate to a broader retrieval or a web source when the local shortlist is weak

use: You can label a golden set that includes no-answer queries
You can monitor abstention rate over time
avoid: Queries are all answerable by construction, such as lookups from a known catalog
You would cut on RRF scores or an uncalibrated constant
A hard refusal frustrates users more than a hedged best-effort answer
flips: Risk rises: tighten the cutoff and prefer abstention
Users complain about too many refusals: add a 'closest matches' fallback instead of a bare refusal
A service model update lands: recalibrate before trusting old thresholds

pitfalls.cause: The service or embedding model changed and the score distribution shifted
pitfalls.fix: Alert on abstention rate and p10, p50, p90 scores. Recalibrate on the golden set

pitfalls.symptom: The bot answers questions the corpus cannot answer
pitfalls.cause: No cutoff, or a threshold on RRF or a miscalibrated absolute score
pitfalls.fix: Cut on reranker or per-leg signals, add unanswerable queries to the golden set

pitfalls.symptom: Users see bare refusals for answerable questions
pitfalls.cause: Cutoff is too strict or the first stage misses the gold chunk
pitfalls.fix: Check recall first, then loosen the cutoff and add a broaden step before abstaining

scenarios.title: Clinical guideline assistant
scenarios.situation: Clinicians ask about dosing and contraindications. The guideline corpus is incomplete, and a wrong dose is a serious risk.
constraints: Corpus does not cover every drug
Latency of a few seconds is fine
scenarios.question: How do you set the cutoff?

options.name: Calibrate a strict cutoff on a golden set with unanswerable queries, abstain with a clear 'not in the guidelines' message and route to a human
options.why: The risk profile prefers missing answers to wrong ones, and the gate is measurable.
options.tradeoff: More abstentions and a human queue.

options.name: Answer from the top 3 chunks and rely on the prompt to hedge
options.why: Hedging does not stop a confident wrong dose.

options.name: Add an LLM judge as the only gate
options.tradeoff: Extra latency and its own error rate, so use it beside a score cutoff.

flips.if: Risk drops, such as a wellness FAQ
flips.then: Loosen the cutoff and show closest matches.

flips.if: The corpus later covers nearly every drug and golden-set coverage is high
flips.then: Keep the strict cutoff but expect fewer abstentions, and keep routing the remaining misses to a human.

scenarios.takeaway: The price of a false answer sets the cutoff.

scenarios.title: Score drift after a service update
scenarios.situation: An absolute reranker cutoff of 2.0 worked for months. After a platform update the assistant abstains on queries that were answered before.
constraints: No release has changed the app
unknowns: Did the embedding model or index change?
scenarios.question: What is the best response?

options.name: Re-run the golden set, recompute coverage and false answers by cutoff, set coarse bands and add drift alerts
options.why: Azure warns the reranker distribution shifts with updates, so calibration must be repeatable [[r3]].

options.name: Lower the cutoff until abstentions stop
options.why: It trades one miscalibration for another and may admit weak chunks.
options.tradeoff: Only a stopgap while the golden set runs.

options.name: Remove the cutoff
options.tradeoff: Brings back fabricated answers for unanswerable queries.

flips.then: Add a relative cutoff or answerability check that moves less with the model.

flips.if: There is no golden set to recalibrate on
flips.then: Build a small labelled set of answerable and unanswerable queries first; until then, fail safe with a conservative cutoff and human review.

scenarios.takeaway: Treat cutoffs as monitored configuration, not constants.

quiz.q: At a cutoff, 170 of 200 answerable queries are answered, and 20 of 100 unanswerable queries are answered anyway. What percentage of all answers given are false?
quiz.hint: False answers divided by all answers given.
quiz.explain: Answers given are 170 + 20 = 190. False answers are 20. 20 / 190 = 10.5%. Coverage on answerable queries is 85%, which is a different measure.

quiz.q: A team cuts on the fused RRF score and abstains on any value below 0.02. Why is this unreliable?
options: RRF reflects rank agreement and list count, not relevance
The vector leg has no weight
quiz.explain: RRF sums 1/(k+rank) terms, so its range depends on the number of lists and `k`. It orders results but does not measure relevance.

quiz.q: Select the actions that make a cutoff safer over time.
options: Include unanswerable queries in the golden set
Recalibrate after model or service updates
quiz.explain: A cutoff needs evidence of both error types, monitoring and recalibration. A hard-coded constant silently decays when score distributions shift.

flashcards.front: Why avoid fine-grained cutoffs on the Azure reranker score?
flashcards.back: The score distribution shifts with infrastructure and model updates, so use coarse bands, monitor and recalibrate.

flashcards.front: How do you calibrate an abstention cutoff?
flashcards.back: Measure coverage and false answers by cutoff on a golden set that includes unanswerable queries, then pick by error cost.
